story.headline: Western states condemn Israel's E1 plan
story.summary: Seven Western governments issued a joint statement calling Israel's opening of E1 West Bank settlement tenders 'unacceptable' and demanding it be retracted.
story.display_body: Seven Western governments issued a joint statement on Thursday 20 August calling Israel's decision to open construction tenders for the E1 West Bank settlement "unacceptable" and demanding it be retracted. The United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Canada and Norway said the E1 project — which would connect occupied East Jerusalem to the Maale Adumim settlement across roughly 12 square kilometres of the West Bank — would "drive a wedge through the West Bank" and harm "the territorial contiguity of the Palestinian Territories", undermining a two-state solution. The statement warned businesses "should not consider bidding" for the tenders, citing "legal and reputational consequences including the risk of involving themselves in serious breaches of international law" — a position it says the UN Security Council has reaffirmed. Israel gave final approval to the E1 plan, slated for at least 3,400 housing units, in August 2025, when Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called it "historic"; the fresh move to publish tenders for more than 1,200 units drew condemnation from the UN secretary-general's office, Egypt and Malaysia as well.
story.why: E1 is the piece of land that, if built on, would sever the northern and southern West Bank from each other and from East Jerusalem — which is why the plan has been frozen for two decades under international pressure, and why its revival is read as closing the door on a contiguous Palestinian state rather than as a routine settlement expansion.

story.headline: North Korea fires 10 missiles
story.summary: North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles a day after the US and South Korea scaled back the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises.
story.display_body: North Korea launched about 10 short-range ballistic missiles toward its eastern waters on Thursday 20 August, a day after the United States and South Korea scaled back their annual joint military exercises. South Korea's joint chiefs said the missiles were fired from the Pyongyang region around 5pm local time; Japan also detected the launches, and Seoul's national security council held an emergency meeting urging Pyongyang to stop tests that are banned under UN Security Council resolutions. The launches followed a US–South Korean decision on Wednesday 19 August to "substantially reduce" the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield drills — an order President Donald Trump gave just before they began on Monday 17 August, citing what he called his good relationship with Kim Jong-un and Seoul's refusal to back him over the war against Iran. Kim Jong-un's influential sister, Kim Yo-jong, had dismissed Trump's overture on Wednesday as not worth commenting on.
story.why: Trump scaled back the drills as a gesture toward reviving diplomacy with Kim; the missile salvo the next day is Pyongyang's answer — pocketing the concession while signalling it feels no pressure to reciprocate.

story.headline: Hong Kong Tiananmen organisers convicted
story.summary: Hong Kong activists Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were found guilty of inciting subversion over the annual Tiananmen vigil.
story.display_body: A Hong Kong court found two organisers of the city's former Tiananmen vigil guilty of "inciting subversion" on Friday 21 August, one of the highest-profile prosecutions under the national security law Beijing imposed in 2020. Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, and Chow Hang-tung, 41 — leaders of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance, which for years ran the annual candlelight vigil marking the 4 June 1989 crackdown in Beijing — were convicted of inciting others to subvert state power by unlawful means; each faces up to 10 years in prison, with sentencing to follow. Their trial ran 24 days from January; a third defendant, former lawmaker Albert Ho, 74, pleaded guilty. Chow, who represented herself, told the court in May that "the law itself was on trial", and the UK Foreign Office condemned the use of the security law to convict the pair.
story.why: Hong Kong and Macau were once the only places on Chinese soil where the Tiananmen dead could be publicly mourned; convicting the vigil's organisers effectively criminalises that memory and marks how far the 2020 security law has reached into ordinary civic life.

story.headline: CAR goldmine collapse kills over 100
story.summary: More than 100 people died when an artisanal goldmine at Zamboye in western Central African Republic caved in from a landslide.
story.display_body: More than 100 people were killed when an artisanal goldmine collapsed in a landslide at Zamboye, in western Central African Republic, on Tuesday 18 August, local officials and aid workers said. The site sits about 50km from the town of Baboua near the Cameroon border; a Red Cross volunteer told the Associated Press that more than 100 bodies had been recovered, and a senior mining-association official gave the same figure to Reuters, though a local prosecutor's statement confirmed only that many miners were trapped without citing a toll. A second prosecutor attributed the disaster to "the collapse of several underground tunnels in which miners were operating", and officials warned the death toll could rise as recovery continues. Authorities have opened an investigation.
story.why: Unregulated artisanal mining — gold here, as with the recurring pit collapses across the Sahel and Central Africa — draws thousands into deep, unsupported tunnels with no safety oversight, so a single landslide can bury more people than many armed clashes in the same region.

story.headline: Neutrality Initiative trails in first SRG poll
story.summary: The first GFS Bern poll on the 27 September federal votes shows Switzerland's Neutrality Initiative headed for rejection and the Food initiative deadlocked.
story.display_body: The first SRG poll on the 27 September federal votes, published Thursday 20 August, shows the Neutrality Initiative headed for defeat and the Food initiative too close to call. In the survey by the GFS Bern institute — conducted 3–16 August among 17,212 eligible voters for public broadcaster SRG SSR — 54 percent said they would reject the "Preservation of Swiss Neutrality" initiative against 42 percent in favour. The initiative, backed by the SVP and allied campaigners, would write a strict, permanent armed neutrality into the constitution, barring Switzerland from military alliances and from joining sanctions against warring states. The parallel Food initiative ("For safe food"), which seeks to lift Switzerland's self-sufficiency toward at least 70 percent through more sustainable and plant-based domestic production, was effectively tied — 49 percent against, 47 percent in favour.
story.why: First polls are trend indicators, not verdicts — but a neutrality initiative that starts 12 points behind faces a steep climb, and its wording (no sanctions against warring states) is precisely what would constrain how Switzerland aligns with EU measures on Russia or Iran, so the September result carries directly into how Bern can act on those files.

story.headline: Thusis fire leaves five missing
story.summary: An overnight fire destroyed a restaurant-and-apartments building in Thusis, Graubünden, leaving five people missing and eight injured.
story.display_body: A fire overnight into Friday 21 August destroyed a building housing a restaurant and apartments in Thusis, in the canton of Graubünden, leaving five people missing and eight injured, cantonal police said. The alarm reached the Graubünden cantonal police shortly after midnight, and nearly 100 firefighters were deployed; 14 people got out of the building, among them the eight injured — two seriously, two with moderate and four with light injuries. According to initial findings the fire started on the building's second floor, and because the stairwell collapsed rescuers had to open the roof with a crane. The block was mainly occupied by individual residents of various nationalities living in small studios; the cantonal police and public prosecutor's office have opened an investigation into the cause.

story.headline: New Swiss reactor could cost up to 43bn francs
story.summary: A Swiss Academies of Sciences report estimates a new nuclear plant would cost 14 to 43 billion francs including financing.
story.display_body: A new report from the Swiss Academies of Sciences estimates that building a nuclear power plant in Switzerland would cost between 14 and 43 billion francs, financing included. The wide range reflects two scenarios and two vendors: in the optimistic case, roughly 14 billion francs for a reactor from the US firm Westinghouse or 21 billion for a larger French EDF model; in the pessimistic case, about 25 billion for the US reactor and 43 billion for the French one. Unlike earlier estimates, the figures fold in capital and financing costs, which could add a further 20–30 percent. The authors conclude such a project would likely be viable only with substantial state backing, since private investors have taken on comparable projects in recent years only where governments absorbed much of the risk.
story.why: Voters lifted Switzerland's ban on building new reactors, so the debate has shifted from whether nuclear is allowed to whether anyone would pay for it; a price tag that only pencils out with heavy public subsidy reframes 'new nuclear' as a fiscal-policy question, not just an energy one.

story.headline: Nvidia strikes $6B Poolside model deal
story.summary: Nvidia agrees a reported non-exclusive $6B licensing deal for Poolside's model-building stack plus a $1B investment; 109 staff get Nvidia offers, founders stay.
story.display_body: Multiple outlets report Nvidia has agreed a non-exclusive $6 billion deal to license the "Model Factory" — the system Poolside (an AI coding-model startup, maker of the Laguna model) uses to build its models — alongside a separate $1 billion investment at a reported $12 billion pre-money valuation. Roughly 109 Poolside staff, largely researchers, are said to be getting Nvidia job offers, while the three founders stay to run Poolside independently. Note the structure, which the reporting stresses: this is not a clean acquisition or acqui-hire — the license is non-exclusive (Poolside can still sell the same technology elsewhere), and Poolside continues as a company. As of writing there is no first-party Nvidia or Poolside press release; the terms rest on sourced reporting.
story.why: it's the window's largest single AI-industry move, and the unusual shape is the story — a chip vendor paying billions to license the model-building capability and hire the people, while leaving the startup standing, rather than buying it outright. It echoes the "reverse-acquihire" pattern regulators have scrutinised in earlier AI deals (structure a talent-and-tech absorption to avoid a merger review), and points to Nvidia moving further up the stack from selling compute toward owning the recipe for frontier models.

story.headline: Robot model learns tasks from one demo
story.summary: Generalist AI's GEN-1.5 performs new physical tasks from a single 3-12s demo with no gradient updates, averaging 59% one-shot success.
story.display_body: Generalist AI released GEN-1.5, an "embodied foundation model" it describes as the first it knows of to show one-shot and few-shot learning of physical skills at scale. A single demonstration of 3–12 seconds is inserted into the model's context as a "physical prompt," and the robot attempts the task immediately, with no gradient update in between — the same in-context learning that makes language models pick up a pattern from a few examples, applied to physical action. It is a multimodal model that ingests video plus sensor, language, and proprioceptive (body-position) input and emits action trajectories at 100 Hz, holding 30 seconds of memory. Across 10 tasks (opening jars, unzipping pouches, retrieving money from a purse), one-shot in-context prompting averaged 59% success straight from pretraining; ten gradient steps on five minutes of data raised that to 83%. The company reports capabilities that emerged from pretraining rather than being trained for — sim-to-real transfer, novel tool use, ambidextrous work. Figures are company-reported and not yet independently reproduced.
story.why: robotics' bottleneck has been data — every new skill traditionally means fresh teleoperation and retraining. If a pretrained model can genuinely acquire a usable skill from one short demo, that changes the economics of deploying robots, which is why commentators are floating a "ChatGPT moment for robotics" framing. Treat that framing as a claim to verify, not a settled result: the 59% one-shot number and the emergent-capability list are the vendor's own.

story.headline: Audit exposes phantom self-improvement gains
story.summary: A control-based audit finds seven measurement artifacts that each invert a reported LLM self-improvement result.
story.display_body: The paper audits a now-common claim: that a model, retrained on its own outputs, has "improved itself." The authors run three rounds of low-rank self-training (rank-32 LoRA — a lightweight fine-tuning method that adjusts a small add-on rather than all the weights) on Qwen3-8B, but critically also push a frozen, untrained copy through the identical measurement pipeline as a control. They find seven distinct measurement failures — several of them standard practice — and each one, on its own, inverts a reported finding when the control is missing. One example: scoring with a single greedy decode (taking the model's top-choice answer once) manufactures apparent capability changes even on the untrained model, largely an artifact of how examples are batched at inference.
story.why: the field increasingly grades self-improvement not by average accuracy but by which specific problems a model newly solves or breaks — and that means subtracting two noisy measurements, exactly where artifacts hide. This is a concrete, reproducible checklist for telling a real gain from a measurement mirage, and a caution that a lot of the "models bootstrapping themselves" literature may be measuring its own pipeline.

story.headline: Anthropic eases enterprise data retention
story.summary: Anthropic plans to let enterprises keep its models' 30-day safety-retention data on their own cloud after customer pushback.
story.display_body: Per sourced reporting, Anthropic intends to let business customers keep the data its most capable models retain on their own cloud infrastructure rather than on Anthropic's — while still requiring a 30-day retention window. This walks back part of a June policy under which Anthropic said it would retain all customer data for its more powerful models for 30 days to detect novel AI-enabled cyberattacks; the company itself acknowledged at the time that the rule would be "unpopular with customers who have come to expect zero retention." The new safety system, developed with 100-plus customers including Salesforce, is expected to roll out later this year. This is a reported plan, not yet a published Anthropic policy.
story.why: data retention is a live procurement and compliance question for anyone deploying frontier models in a regulated or privacy-sensitive setting — including Swiss and EU enterprises bound by strict data-handling rules. The move shows the safety-vs-confidentiality tension being negotiated in the open, with a "keep it on your own cloud" compromise as the emerging middle ground (OpenAI is reported to be testing a similar "private safety processing" approach).

story.headline: Agent memory fails at state tracking
story.summary: StateMemBench shows LLM memory systems often answer with superseded facts when world state is revised over a long interaction.
story.display_body: Most memory benchmarks test recall — can the agent fetch a fact it saw earlier. This paper argues that real deployments need state tracking: as facts, constraints, and decisions get revised over a long interaction, the answer must reflect the current state, not a superseded one. StateMemBench is 234 multi-session scenarios with closed-pool grading that explicitly scores whether an answer reflects the current state, a stale (superseded) state, or neither — separating "tracked the wrong version" from other errors by construction. Existing memory systems find it hard.
story.why: the single most common way a long-running assistant goes wrong is confidently acting on something you changed three turns ago. Naming and measuring that failure mode — distinct from ordinary recall — gives memory-system builders a target that matches how agents actually break in production.

story.headline: Coding agents struggle on science code
story.summary: SWE-bench Science, 119 tasks across 20 scientific domains, finds even the best coding agent (Claude Code with Opus-5) passes under 50% first try.
story.display_body: SWE-bench Science is a repository-level benchmark of 119 tasks from 98 GitHub repositories across 20 scientific domains, sorted into three paradigms (issue-driven, expert-exploratory, engineering-integration). The framing is that scientific software is part of the instrument — a bug can corrupt the evidence, not just the program. The headline result: even the strongest agent tested, Claude Code with Opus-5 (max), lands a pass@1 below 50% (pass@1 = solves it on the first attempt). A paired ablation finds scientific guidance is not uniformly helpful — well-grounded context helps, but poorly aligned guidance can anchor the agent onto a wrong repair.
story.why: the reader works in software, and "can a coding agent fix a real repo" is the concrete version of the agent-hype question. A sub-50% first-try rate on scientific code — where domain knowledge and correctness both bite — is a sober, well-measured counterweight to leaderboard-topping SWE-bench numbers, and the failure taxonomy is a practical guide to where these agents break.

story.headline: Model learns when to think
story.summary: An RL method lets a reasoning model pick NoThink/Short/Long modes per problem, cutting tokens 41% at near-equal accuracy.
story.display_body: Reasoning models usually run at a fixed token budget, over-thinking easy problems and under-thinking hard ones. This paper lets the model pick, as its first token, one of three modes — NoThink, Short, or Long — learned inside GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, the reward-based post-training recipe behind recent reasoning models) with no separate router, using a shaped reward plus hard per-mode token caps. On a 1.5B model trained on MATH the modes emerge without collapsing, and accuracy holds (0.782 vs 0.796 base on held-out MATH500) while mean response length drops from 4,796 to 2,811 tokens — a 41% cut. It transfers untrained to other benchmarks, e.g. 76% fewer tokens on GSM8K.
story.why: inference cost is roughly proportional to tokens generated, so a model that spends effort in proportion to difficulty — and learns the dial itself, rather than a hand-set "reasoning effort" slider — is a cheap, broadly reusable efficiency lever.

story.headline: Fine-tuning teaches sparse attention to forget
story.summary: An AWS method co-adapts a model to any KV-cache sparse-attention policy on a single A100, often beating exact attention.
story.display_body: Long-context inference is bottlenecked by the KV cache (the stored keys/values for every past token, whose size grows with context). Sparse-attention policies drop most of it to save memory, but the model was never trained to expect that. This method fine-tunes a model to co-adapt with any KV-cache policy, runs on a single 40 GB A100, and often ends up more accurate than a model trained with exact attention. It ships an efficient kernel for H2O (a leading "keep the heavy-hitter tokens" policy) and open-source code, KeysAndValues (github.com/awslabs/keys_values).
story.why: most sparse-attention work bolts the shortcut onto a model at inference and eats an accuracy hit; training the model to live with the shortcut on a single GPU is a practical recipe for cheaper long-context serving — directly relevant to anyone running long-context models on modest hardware.

fields.display_body: Long-context inference is bottlenecked by the KV cache (the stored keys/values for every past token, whose size grows with context). Sparse-attention policies drop most of it to save memory, but the model was never trained to expect that. This method fine-tunes a model to co-adapt with any KV-cache policy, runs on a single 40 GB A100, and often ends up more accurate than a model trained with exact attention. It ships an efficient kernel for H2O (a leading "keep the heavy-hitter tokens" policy) and open-source code, KeysAndValues (github.com/awslabs/keys_values).
fields.why: most sparse-attention work bolts the shortcut onto a model at inference and eats an accuracy hit; training the model to live with the shortcut on a single GPU is a practical recipe for cheaper long-context serving — directly relevant to anyone running long-context models on modest hardware.

story.headline: Single-rollout method sharpens agentic RL
story.summary: SAPO shares one autoregressive backbone for policy and value, beating PPO and GRPO on agent tasks while dropping the separate critic.
story.display_body: Agentic reinforcement learning trains a model over long, multi-step tasks. Critic-free methods like GRPO estimate how good an action was from several sampled rollouts, dodging the memory cost of PPO's separate value network — but they assign credit poorly over long horizons and can suffer "advantage collapse." SAPO folds the policy and value function into one shared autoregressive backbone (predicting both at different points in the same generation), and adds a trajectory-level advantage estimator for per-turn credit. On ALFWorld and WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B it beats PPO and GRPO by mean +15.1 and +12.1 points while cutting per-iteration runtime 33.2% versus PPO and dropping the separate critic entirely. This is a distinct line from the token-level credit-assignment work covered last edition, converging on the same problem from the value-estimation side.
story.why: temporal credit assignment — figuring out which step in a long task deserved the reward — is the central difficulty in training agents, and doing it without a memory-hungry critic is exactly the lever that makes agentic RL affordable to run.

story.headline: Relevant memories can trap model reasoning
story.summary: MemTrapBench shows faithfully stored, relevant memories can still distort reasoning and hurt current-task accuracy.
story.display_body: The companion failure mode to state-tracking. MemTrapBench shows that even memories that are faithfully recorded and semantically relevant can distort a model's reasoning or beliefs and drag down performance on the task in front of it. The authors define two "cognitive traps": Reasoning Fixation (a retrieved memory locks the model onto a prior line of thought it should abandon) and Belief Distortion (a memory shifts what the model treats as true). Both show up across two model families.
story.why: the reflexive fix for agent errors is "give it more memory / better retrieval." This is evidence that more retrieved context is not free — the wrong-but-relevant memory is a live hazard, not just missing memory — which argues for memory systems that decide whether to use a retrieved item, not only how to fetch it.

story.headline: Benchmark tests AI self-improvement design
story.summary: AI4AI-Bench asks LLM agents to design better training algorithms across 10 frozen research repositories, isolating the crux of recursive self-improvement.
story.display_body: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) — the idea that an AI could improve the process that builds AIs, so each generation inherits the gain — hinges on one specific ability: can an agent design a better training algorithm (a better objective or update rule), as opposed to just collecting more data or tuning hyperparameters? AI4AI-Bench isolates exactly that, with 10 frozen research repositories spanning 10 training-algorithm families; a change counts only if it alters how the model learns, not how a run is executed. The authors argue no prior suite separates those two.
story.why: "recursive self-improvement" is invoked constantly in AI-risk and AGI-timeline debates, usually without a way to measure it. Pairing this with Phantom Gains above, the cycle's message is consistent: the burden of proof on self-improvement claims is being raised, and the honest current answer is "not yet, and here's how we'll know."

story.headline: LLMs falter on frontier theory research
story.summary: FormalTCS, 175 Lean-formalized tasks from STOC/FOCS/SODA/COLT, finds autoformalization the sharpest bottleneck for LLM theory research.
story.display_body: FormalTCS tests whether LLMs can do realistic theoretical-computer-science research: 175 instances drawn from papers accepted to STOC, FOCS, SODA, and COLT (the top theory venues) in 2025–2026, each with an expert-verified Lean formalization (Lean is a proof assistant that machine-checks mathematical proofs). The bottleneck is autoformalization — turning a natural-language claim into a formal theorem statement: the best model scores just 11.5 there, versus 28.6 (Pass@8) when instead asked to prove a human-provided formal statement. Worse, when the framework generates its own new claims, only 6 of 64 survive expert evaluation and proof — so "research taste" is a second wall beyond formalization.
story.why: amid claims that models are nearing autonomous mathematical research, this pins down two concrete, separable failures — models can't reliably even state the problem formally, and can't reliably tell a good conjecture from a bad one. It's a precise, honestly-scoped map of the gap.
